demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
At 22 years old, Miguel Martinez found himself trapped in the aftermath of a tragic accident that forever altered his life. As an HVAC technician, he had enjoyed the hands-on nature of his work, relishing the satisfaction of solving problems in various buildings. However, one fateful day, while working on a rooftop unit, he accidentally caused a serious injury to a co-worker, who fell and broke his leg severely. The sight of his colleague writhing in pain, coupled with the realization of his role in the incident, left Miguel grappling with a profound sense of guilt and despair. He couldn’t shake the feeling that he had failed to protect someone he considered a friend. Over time, this guilt morphed into a belief that he was an unreliable person, leading him to view his body as a traitor that had let him down at the most critical moment. He began to adopt maladaptive strategies, convinced that avoiding situations where he might fail was the only rational way to protect himself from further shame and disappointment. This belief drove him to adopt maladaptive strategies, as he felt that avoiding situations where he might fail was the only way to protect himself from further shame and disappointment. His negative self-view convinced him that by avoiding potential stressors, he was safeguarding himself from the inevitable failures that would only reinforce his feelings of inadequacy. This belief that he was weak and inadequate made the memories of the accident more vivid, as if they were always waiting for him to revisit the moment of his failure, reinforcing his negative self-view. With each painful recollection, Miguel felt a surge of anxiety, leading him to believe that the danger he had experienced was not just a past event, but an ever-present threat that could return at any moment.

In the months following the accident, Miguel developed maladaptive strategies to cope with his overwhelming feelings. He began to avoid any dates or anniversaries related to the event, fearing that even a simple mention of the accident would plunge him back into the guilt and shame he felt. Yet, each time he avoided reminders of the incident, he felt a growing sense of fragility, convincing himself that he could not handle the emotional weight of the memories, which only deepened his negative self-appraisal. This avoidance extended to stressful situations in general; he would often decline social invitations or skip work if he sensed the day might be difficult, believing that staying away would protect him from feeling like a failure again. Yet, deep down, he recognized that this avoidance only reinforced his negative self-appraisal. With every instance of retreating from potentially stressful situations, his internal narrative grew louder, whispering that he must be weaker than others who could face their fears, further embedding his feelings of inadequacy. Each time he chose to evade a triggering situation, he felt a quiet confirmation of his belief that he was incapable of handling stress, further embedding the notion that he was weak and inadequate. Each time he chose to evade a triggering situation, he felt a quiet confirmation of his belief that he was incapable of handling stress, further embedding the notion that he was weak and inadequate. He viewed his decision to retreat from social situations as a necessary safeguard, convinced that if he faced the world, he would only be reminded of his perceived failures and the threat they represented. He felt as though he was retreating from life, furthering the belief that he was unrecognizable and diminished from the person he once was.

Miguel's memories of the accident haunted him relentlessly. He often found himself trapped in an agonizing loop, replaying the events over and over in his mind, trying to make sense of how it could have happened. These memories felt alien, as if they belonged to someone else. The moment he thought about the incident, he would inexplicably catch a whiff of the metallic smell of the tools he used that day, instantly transporting him back to that rooftop and the horror of the accident. Unable to control the intrusive memories, Miguel experienced a heightened sense of threat. The silence in his apartment became deafening, triggering a fear that something dangerous might be lurking just out of sight, ready to pounce. This heightened sense of threat kept the memories of the accident close to the surface, as if they were a necessary reminder of the danger he felt was always present, forcing him to relive the event repeatedly. The recollections not only brought back the guilt but also intensified his feeling of vulnerability, as he was certain that each memory was a signal of an imminent danger, lurking just beneath the surface of his reality. Once the memories emerged, they left Miguel with an acute sense of threat, as he felt the danger was not confined to the past; it was as if the trauma had become an ever-present, lurking specter in his life. Each recollection intensified his perception of threat, leading him to believe that the past was not something he could escape; instead, it had rooted itself firmly in his present reality. Once the memories surfaced, they influenced his perception of threat, convincing him that danger was not a thing of the past but an ever-present risk that he had to remain vigilant against.

This constant threat perception further exacerbated Miguel's memory disturbances. Every time he was reminded of the accident, whether by a sound, a sight, or even an unremarkable silence, it would force the memory back into his consciousness. He had come to associate unexpected quiet with impending danger, fueling his anxiety and making his environment feel perilous. Consequently, he sought refuge in familiar places that felt safe, yet he realized that this self-imposed limitation on his life only deepened his belief that he was fragile and untrustworthy. His constant avoidance left him with no evidence that the world outside was safe, reinforcing his perception of an ongoing threat that loomed just beyond his self-imposed barriers. By never allowing himself to confront the world outside, he never had the chance to discover that the dangers he feared were often unfounded, which kept his sense of threat perpetually high and unchallenged. By never allowing himself to confront the outside world, he inadvertently perpetuated the sense of threat, convincing himself that the dangers he feared were valid and ever-present, rather than testing the reality of his beliefs. His constant avoidance of situations that might challenge his beliefs about himself left him without the opportunity to discover safety, which only solidified the idea that the threats he perceived were real and ongoing. By avoiding situations that might trigger his memories, he unwittingly solidified his belief that danger was a constant, never allowing himself the opportunity to discover that the outside world could be safe and supportive.

In grappling with these emotions, Miguel felt as if he were spiraling deeper into a cycle of self-reproach. His maladaptive strategies bred further negative appraisals, leaving him feeling trapped in a cycle he could not escape. The very actions he took to avoid stress and discomfort only served to heighten his feelings of guilt and inadequacy, creating an unending loop of fear and regret. He recognized that his life was shrinking around him, and the world felt increasingly dangerous.

Finally, after months of isolation and turmoil, Miguel reached a breaking point. He could no longer tolerate the weight of his guilt and fear. The thought of seeking help filled him with trepidation, yet he found himself hoping that perhaps, through therapy, he might learn to forgive himself and navigate the memories that felt so alien. He was terrified of what confronting his trauma might entail, yet he longed to reclaim the person he once was, to step back into life without the incessant shadow of the accident looming over him. It was this fragile hope that finally drove Miguel to seek professional help, yearning to understand how to reconcile his painful past with the possibility of a brighter future.

REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals influence or lead to memory disturbances.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show that the perceived threat influences or causes memory disturbances.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette lacks a causal connection where maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not demonstrate that maladaptive strategies contribute to or exacerbate the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
